```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")

summary_cache <- jsonlite::fromJSON("early_african_islands_summary_cache.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
settlements_raw <- jsonlite::fromJSON("early_african_islands_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

subregs <- summary_cache$subregions
sub_by_id <- setNames(subregs, vapply(subregs, function (x) x$id, character(1)))
dist_by_id <- setNames(
  summary_cache$subregion_settlement_distribution,
  vapply(summary_cache$subregion_settlement_distribution, function (x) x$id, character(1))
)

n_total_sites <- as.integer(summary_cache$settlement_count)
n_excluded_sites <- as.integer(summary_cache$wave_saturation_stats$ledger_excluded)
n_candidate_sites <- n_total_sites + n_excluded_sites
n_obs_total <- as.integer(summary_cache$observation_count)
total_area_km2 <- as.numeric(summary_cache$total_area_km2)
total_pixels <- as.integer(summary_cache$total_pixels)

bench_keys <- c("0", "800", "1400", "1700", "1810", "1890")
headline_vals <- vapply(bench_keys, function (k) as.numeric(summary_cache$headline_series[[k]]), numeric(1))

subregion_order <- c(
  "merina_central_highlands",
  "betsileo_southern_highlands",
  "betsimisaraka_east_madagascar",
  "antandroy_mahafaly_south_mdg",
  "sakalava_menabe_boina",
  "mascarenes_mauritius_reunion",
  "comoros_sultanates_mayotte",
  "cabo_verde_atlantic",
  "sao_tome_principe_st_helena",
  "seychelles_chagos_wio"
)

fmt_era_yr <- function (y) {
  yi <- as.integer(y)
  if (yi < 0L) paste0(abs(yi), "BC") else if (yi == 0L) "1AD" else paste0(yi, "AD")
}
```

# Abstract

Between 500BC and 1895AD, maritime colonisation across the western Indian Ocean and the Portuguese and British islands of the African Atlantic transformed previously uninhabited or lightly settled archipelagos into dense agrarian, mercantile and plantation societies. Across a territorial domain of `r viscount_fmt_number(total_area_km2, 0L)` km² spanning ten modern island states and overseas territories, NICETHI reconstructs a gridded regional population moving from `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["0"]])` inhabitants at 1AD and a third-century trough of `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["300"]])` at 300AD to `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["800"]])` at 800AD, `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1400"]])` at 1400AD, `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1700"]])` at 1700AD, `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1810"]])` at 1810AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1890"]])` by 1890AD, reaching a mean end-epoch density of `r viscount_fmt_number(summary_cache$end_epoch_density_km2, 2L)` persons/km² on the 5-arcminute grid. Growth followed two oceanic rhythms. In the western Indian Ocean, Austronesian outrigger voyagers and East African Bantu-speaking farmers and Swahili mariners settled the Comoros and Madagascar, building coral-stone entrepots at Mahilaka, Vohemar, Domoni and Dembéni before irrigated highland rice terraces sustained the Merina kingdom centred on Antananarivo. On uninhabited oceanic islands, European maritime expansion after 1460AD forged plantation and entrepot societies: sugar and slave-trading depots in Cabo Verde and São Tomé e Príncipe, followed by slave-worked coffee and sugar estates and post-emancipation Indian indentured migration across Mauritius and Réunion. Grounded in `r viscount_fmt_number(n_total_sites, 0L)` individually assessed settlements across `r viscount_fmt_number(n_obs_total, 0L)` chronological observations, colonial island censuses and sub-regional spatial disaggregation, this chapter reconciles gridded macro-series with archival enumeration from Ribeira Grande to Port-Louis.

```{r fig1-md-only, results='asis'}

    "fig:hero-african-islands"
  )
}
```

# Background

## Austronesian Voyages, Swahili Ports and Malagasy State Formation

The islands flanking Africa fall into two distinct demographic worlds. On the eastern side, Madagascar and the Comoros lie close enough to the East African coast and within the reach of Indian Ocean monsoon currents to have absorbed pre-European agrarian settlement, yet distant enough to preserve a remarkable linguistic and ecological synthesis [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar]. Settlers arriving from southern Borneo across the northern Indian Ocean rim introduced wet-rice cultivation, outrigger navigation, bananas, taro and Malagasy speech, while Bantu-speaking migrants crossing the Mozambique Channel brought cattle pastoralism, sorghum, ironworking and Swahili coastal links [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. Archaeological surveys across northern and southern Madagascar document permanent coastal towns and interior fortified hilltop villages by the tenth to thirteenth centuries AD, led by Mahilaka on Ampasindava Bay, Vohemar on the north-east littoral, Talaky and Andranosoa in the arid south, and Dembéni and Sima in the Comoros [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas].

Between 1500AD and 1800AD, maritime firearms imports, Indian Ocean cloth exchange and cattle raiding reorganised Malagasy politics around regional dynasties [@Berg1985TheSacred; @Grandidier1885HistoirePhysique]. Along the western plains, Sakalava monarchs at Menabe and Boina (Boeny, Kingany, Marovoay and later Mahajanga) taxed Swahili-Arab and European shipping, whereas the Betsimisaraka confederation unified eastern littoral ports around Ambodifototra on Île Sainte-Marie and Mahavelona [@Escamps1858HistoireGeographie; @Berg1985TheSacred]. On the central plateau, Merina rulers expanded hydraulic rice dikes across the Ikopa marshes around Alasora, Ambohimanga and Antananarivo [@Raison1977PerceptionRealisation; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. Under Andrianampoinimerina and Radama I after 1790AD, highland unification turned Antananarivo into a royal capital commanding tribute, conscripted corvée labour (*fanompoana*), and slave exports and imports across the island [@Larson2000HistoryMemory; @Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar].

## Oceanic Plantations, Atlantic Entrepots and Archival Historiography

In contrast to Madagascar and the Comoros, the Mascarenes (Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues), the granitic Seychelles, the Chagos atolls, Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe, Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha were uninhabited when Portuguese, Dutch, French and British vessels charted them between 1460AD and 1660AD [@Oliver1950TheVoyage; @Seibert2014CrioulizacaoCabo]. Their human history began as an abrupt colonial experiment. Portuguese settlers peopled Santiago in Cabo Verde from 1462AD and São Tomé from the 1480s with metropolitan colonists, Genoese merchants, exiled convicts and enslaved West and Central Africans [@Seibert2014CrioulizacaoCabo; @Fonju2021ToticPortuguese]. São Tomé pioneered the Atlantic sugar-plantation complex in the sixteenth century before Dutch raids, maroon resistance by the Angolares and Brazilian competition redirected Portuguese plantation capital westward [@Seibert2014CrioulizacaoCabo; @Berthet2016SaoTome]. Cabo Verde meanwhile developed a dry-land agropastoral and slave-provisioning society anchored at Ribeira Grande (Cidade Velha) and later Praia and Mindelo, repeatedly devastated by Sahelian droughts and famines [@Pereira2024RecensaoSantos; @Keese2024BetweenLand].

In the Mascarenes, brief seventeenth-century Dutch occupation on Mauritius gave way to French settlement on Île Bourbon (Réunion) from 1665AD and Île de France (Mauritius) from 1721AD [@Oliver1950TheVoyage]. Under Mahé de La Bourdonnais, Port-Louis and Saint-Denis became naval and commercial hubs fed by enslaved labourers drawn from Madagascar and Mozambique [@Larson2000HistoryMemory; @Allen1999SlavesFreedmen]. Following British capture in 1810AD and the abolition of slavery in 1835AD on Mauritius and 1848AD on Réunion, sugar estates imported hundreds of thousands of indentured workers from British India, doubling island populations within a generation [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen]. Historiography for these archipelagos has shifted from nineteenth-century colonial chronicles [@Escamps1858HistoireGeographie; @Grandidier1885HistoirePhysique] and travel accounts [@Oliver1950TheVoyage] to archival demographic analysis of parish rolls, ecclesiastical registers, slave compensation returns and post-emancipation labour censuses [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen; @Larson2000HistoryMemory; @Pereira2024RecensaoSantos; @Rodrigues2011RecensaoBelinquete]. NICETHI brings these archaeological surveys and colonial census series into a single quantitative baseline spanning 500BC to 1895AD.

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partition and Oceanic Accounting Domain

The study area spans `r viscount_fmt_number(total_area_km2, 0L)` km² across `r viscount_fmt_number(total_pixels, 0L)` five-arcminute grid cells covering ten modern jurisdictions: Madagascar, Mauritius, Réunion, Comoros, Mayotte, Seychelles, British Indian Ocean Territory (Chagos), Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe, and Saint Helena (including Ascension and Tristan da Cunha). Within NICETHI, the chapter occupies Regime 2 (-500 to 1895), bridging early Austronesian-Bantu island colonisation with high colonial sugar plantations and late nineteenth-century imperial conquest. Ten sub-regions partition the territory using OpenHistoricalMap polity footprints, HydroBASINS Level-6 watersheds across Madagascar, Nunn-Murdock ethnographic zones and geoBoundaries coastal outlines [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] (Table \ref{tab:subregions}).

```{r tab1-subregions, results='asis'}
df_t1 <- data.frame(
  Subregion = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) sub_by_id[[id]]$name, character(1)),
  `Area (km²)` = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) viscount_fmt_number(sub_by_id[[id]]$area_km2, 0L), character(1)),
  Pixels = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) viscount_fmt_number(sub_by_id[[id]]$pixel_count, 0L), character(1)),
  Era = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) {
    pts <- strsplit(as.character(sub_by_id[[id]]$era), "\\.\\.")[[1]]
    paste0(fmt_era_yr(pts[1]), "-", fmt_era_yr(pts[2]))
  }, character(1)),
  `Assessed Sites` = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) viscount_fmt_number(dist_by_id[[id]]$settlement_count, 0L), character(1)),
  `Share (%)` = vapply(subregion_order, function (id) viscount_fmt_number(100 * sub_by_id[[id]]$area_km2 / total_area_km2, 1L), character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_t1) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_t1,
  "Ten ecological and political sub-regions of the African islands study area, showing surface area, 5-arcminute pixel counts, regional eras and assessed settlements.",
  arg3_options = list(label = "tab:subregions")
)
```

Five sub-regions divide Madagascar into ecological and political zones: the Kingdom of Imerina on the central highlands, the Betsileo southern plateau, the eastern Betsimisaraka littoral and Île Sainte-Marie, the western Sakalava kingdoms of Menabe and Boina, and the arid southern chiefdoms of Antandroy, Mahafaly and Anosy. Five insular sub-regions group the neighbouring archipelagos: the Mascarenes (Mauritius, Réunion and Rodrigues), the Comoros sultanates and Mayotte, Portuguese Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe paired with South Atlantic Saint Helena, and the granitic Seychelles, Chagos and Îles Éparses.

## Settlement Screening, Census Sources and Archival Calibration

To reconstruct urban and port trajectories, `r viscount_fmt_number(n_candidate_sites, 0L)` candidate archaeological sites, coral-stone towns, royal hilltops and colonial port municipalities between 500BC and 1895AD were screened from excavation inventories, East India Company muster rolls and national statistical archives [@ICM2020MadagascarAtlas; @Allen1999SlavesFreedmen; @Grandidier1885HistoirePhysique]. Removing `r viscount_fmt_number(n_excluded_sites, 0L)` duplicate alias record (a redundant entry for Antananarivo) left `r viscount_fmt_number(n_total_sites, 0L)` individually assessed settlements across `r viscount_fmt_number(n_obs_total, 0L)` chronological observations (Figure \ref{fig:hero-african-islands}). Every entry carries a city-proper scope (96 city-proper, 0 metropolitan agglomerations) so compact urban towns are not conflated with rural parish boundaries.

Where pre-colonial archaeological sites lack written enumerations, headcounts are anchored to surveyed site footprints and pre-industrial African urban density benchmarks: Storey's 59-city survey gives a mean density of 12.724 persons/km² and median 10.000 persons/km², while Agbaje-Williams's Yoruba transect calibrates compound occupation at 60 to 88 persons/ha. At Mahilaka on Madagascar's north-western bay, the 20 ha walled stone core yields 3.850 inhabitants by 1150AD and 6.250 at its 1300AD apogee [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. At Antananarivo, an 88 ha mid-nineteenth-century walled and terraced core combines with early missionary and Merina court estimates to trace growth from 4.200 in 1620AD and 18.500 in 1794AD to a temporary royal-muster peak of 75k in 1817AD before stabilising around 48k to 52k between 1828AD and 1895AD [@Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar; @Larson2000HistoryMemory].

For European-administered islands, French East India Company returns (1735, 1767, 1788, 1806), British colonial censuses for Mauritius, Seychelles and Saint Helena (1846 to 1891), Portuguese *Anuário Estatístico do Ultramar* returns for Cabo Verde and São Tomé e Príncipe (1731 to 1878), and INSEE/Mauritius Central Statistics Office series supply direct port and parish enumerations [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen; @Seibert2014CrioulizacaoCabo; @Fonju2021ToticPortuguese]. Gridded rural populations across the 5-arcminute raster draw on non-stationary Matérn residual interpolation over combined HYDE 3.5 and KK10 agricultural baselines, constrained by sub-regional historical polity totals and geoBoundaries administrative polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries].

# Testing and Validation

## Colonial Island Censuses and Gridded Raster Reconciliation

Cross-checking the 5-arcminute gridded totals against historical island censuses exposes an essential scale effect between large continental-shelf Madagascar and small volcanic islands (Table \ref{tab:island-censuses}). Across Madagascar, Merina-era estimates of roughly 2,5M around 1800AD [@Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar] and the 1900 French colonial estimate of 2,24M (2.244.872) align closely with NICETHI's five Malagasy sub-regions, which sum to `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["merina_central_highlands"]]$population[["1810"]] + sub_by_id[["betsileo_southern_highlands"]]$population[["1810"]] + sub_by_id[["betsimisaraka_east_madagascar"]]$population[["1810"]] + sub_by_id[["antandroy_mahafaly_south_mdg"]]$population[["1810"]] + sub_by_id[["sakalava_menabe_boina"]]$population[["1810"]])` in 1810AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["merina_central_highlands"]]$population[["1890"]] + sub_by_id[["betsileo_southern_highlands"]]$population[["1890"]] + sub_by_id[["betsimisaraka_east_madagascar"]]$population[["1890"]] + sub_by_id[["antandroy_mahafaly_south_mdg"]]$population[["1890"]] + sub_by_id[["sakalava_menabe_boina"]]$population[["1890"]])` in 1890AD.

```{r tab2-island-censuses, results='asis'}
df_t2 <- data.frame(
  Polity = c(
    "Madagascar (Merina Era)",
    "Madagascar (French Colony)",
    "Cabo Verde Archipelago",
    "Cabo Verde Archipelago",
    "Île de France (Mauritius)",
    "Mauritius Colony (10 Districts)",
    "Mauritius Colony (10 Districts)",
    "Île Bourbon (Réunion)",
    "Île Bonaparte (Réunion)",
    "La Réunion Colony",
    "São Tomé e Príncipe"
  ),
  Year = c("1800AD", "1900AD", "1878AD", "1900AD", "1735AD", "1851AD", "1891AD", "1735AD", "1806AD", "1881AD", "1900AD"),
  `Enumerated Pop.` = c(
    "2,5M", "2,24M", "99,3k", "147,4k", "838", "181,3k", "372,7k", "8,3k", "65k", "170,5k", "42,1k"
  ),
  `Primary Archival Record` = c(
    "Campbell (1991); INSTAT synthesis",
    "Gouvernement Général 1900 estimate",
    "Anuário Estatístico do Ultramar",
    "Anuário Estatístico do Ultramar",
    "French East India Company census",
    "British Colonial Census (Statoids)",
    "British Colonial Census (Statoids)",
    "French East India Company census",
    "Colonial Mascarenes census",
    "INSEE Recensement de La Réunion",
    "Anuário Estatístico do Ultramar"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_t2) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_t2,
  "Historical island-wide census and administrative population benchmarks across Madagascar, Cabo Verde, Mauritius, Réunion and São Tomé e Príncipe.",
  arg3_options = list(label = "tab:island-censuses")
)
```

On the small oceanic islands, however, five-arcminute spatial grids (roughly 85 km² per cell near the equator) under-represent compact plantation colonies because coastal pixel masking removes steep or narrow littoral cells and splits tiny atolls into sub-pixel land fractions. Thus, while the 5-arcminute raster records `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["mascarenes_mauritius_reunion"]]$population[["1890"]])` for the Mascarenes in 1890AD, `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["cabo_verde_atlantic"]]$population[["1890"]])` for Cabo Verde and zero gridded rural inhabitants on the 107 marine-dominated cells of Seychelles and Chagos, full colonial enumerations establish 372,7k residents in Mauritius in 1891AD, 170,5k in Réunion in 1881AD, 99,3k in Cabo Verde in 1878AD and 42,1k in São Tomé e Príncipe by 1900AD [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen; @Berthet2016SaoTome]. The district-level British censuses of Mauritius in 1851AD and 1891AD (Table \ref{tab:mauritius-districts}) illustrate this rapid interior densification directly: Port-Louis grew modestly from 49,9k to 62,2k, whereas sugar and railway districts such as Plaines Wilhems (13,9k to 57,6k), Moka (5,7k to 32,6k), Savanne (9,9k to 35k) and Flacq (24,2k to 56,7k) tripled or quadrupled as Indian indentured families settled beyond the port [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen].

```{r tab3-mauritius-districts, results='asis'}
mus_1851 <- Filter(function (x) identical(x$polity_code, "MUS") && x$year == 1851, summary_cache$subadmin_benchmark_tables)[[1]]$units
mus_1891 <- Filter(function (x) identical(x$polity_code, "MUS") && x$year == 1891, summary_cache$subadmin_benchmark_tables)[[1]]$units
u91_map <- setNames(vapply(mus_1891, function (u) as.numeric(u$population), numeric(1)), vapply(mus_1891, function (u) u$unit_name, character(1)))

df_t3 <- data.frame(
  District = vapply(mus_1851, function (u) as.character(u$unit_name), character(1)),
  `1851AD` = vapply(mus_1851, function (u) viscount_fmt_pop(u$population), character(1)),
  `1891AD` = vapply(mus_1851, function (u) viscount_fmt_pop(u91_map[[u$unit_name]]), character(1)),
  `Growth (%)` = vapply(mus_1851, function (u) {
    p51 <- as.numeric(u$population)
    p91 <- u91_map[[u$unit_name]]
    viscount_fmt_number(100 * (p91 - p51) / p51, 1L)
  }, character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_t3 <- rbind(df_t3, data.frame(
  District = "Mauritius Total",
  `1851AD` = viscount_fmt_pop(181318),
  `1891AD` = viscount_fmt_pop(372656),
  `Growth (%)` = viscount_fmt_number(100 * (372656 - 181318) / 181318, 1L),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))
rownames(df_t3) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_t3,
  "Enumerated district populations across Mauritius (including Rodrigues) in the 1851AD and 1891AD British colonial censuses.",
  arg3_options = list(label = "tab:mauritius-districts")
)
```

## Settlement Rank-Size Calibration and Ledger Saturation

Across all `r viscount_fmt_number(n_total_sites, 0L)` individually assessed settlements, ordinary least-squares rank-size regression on the upper half (n=48) yields a Zipf exponent of $q = 0,866$ ($R^2 = 0,9856$), while full-sample regression across all 492 entries produces $q = 1,088$ ($R^2 = 0,8308$) with a unique-peak ratio of 0,7604 and log-interquartile spread of 0,528 (Figure \ref{fig:rank-size}). An upper-half slope below unity ($q = 0,87$) reflects a bi-coastal archipelago system shared by twin leading capitals, Antananarivo (75k peak in 1817AD) in highland Madagascar and Port-Louis (74,5k peak in 1861AD) in Mauritius, supported by secondary colonial ports in Réunion (Saint-Denis 36,1k; Saint-Pierre 27,8k; Saint-Paul 24,9k; Saint-Benoît 16,2k; Saint-Louis 14,7k; Saint-André 13,8k) and regional Malagasy hubs (Mahajanga 14,2k; Toamasina 10,2k; Fianarantsoa 9,4k).

```{r fig3-rank-size, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig_03_rank_size.png",
  "Settlement rank-size distribution across 96 island settlements (q = 0,87, R² = 0,99) and mean gridded sub-regional population densities in 1890AD.",
  "fig:rank-size",
  arg3_options = list(max_height = "0.38\\textheight")
)
```

Four structured screening waves reached zero marginal gain (0% addition in Wave 4) with zero empty inhabited sub-regions (10/10 covered) and zero crowd-sourced or fallback compendium dependencies. Beyond rank 50, smaller Cabo Verdean ports, Comorian townlets, Seychellois districts, Chagos copra camps and South Atlantic garrisons (ranging from 109 at Edinburgh of the Seven Seas on Tristan da Cunha to 1,94k at Antsohihy and Le Port) create the steeper lower tail visible in Figure \ref{fig:rank-size}.

# Results

## Austronesian-Bantu Settlement and Mediaeval Trade Ports (1AD to 1400AD)

At 1AD, the gridded regional baseline records `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["0"]])` inhabitants across the islands before dropping sharply to `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["300"]])` at 300AD and recovering to `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["600"]])` by 600AD (Table \ref{tab:trajectory} and Figure \ref{fig:trends}). This early trough mirrors sparse initial archaeological visibility prior to sustained Iron Age village formation, followed by rapid Austronesian and Bantu agrarian expansion between 600AD and 1100AD [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. By 800AD, regional population reached `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["800"]])`, led by central highland Imerina (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["merina_central_highlands"]]$population[["800"]])`), Betsileo (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["betsileo_southern_highlands"]]$population[["800"]])`), the eastern Betsimisaraka littoral (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["betsimisaraka_east_madagascar"]]$population[["800"]])`) and southern Madagascar (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["antandroy_mahafaly_south_mdg"]]$population[["800"]])`), while Comorian sultanate precursors held `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["comoros_sultanates_mayotte"]]$population[["800"]])`.

```{r fig2-trends, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig_02_trends.png",
  "Regional and attested urban population trajectories, active settlement counts and five leading urban centres across the island regions from 1AD to 1895AD.",
  "fig:trends",
  arg3_options = list(max_height = "0.38\\textheight")
)
```

From 800AD to 1400AD, Indian Ocean monsoon commerce integrated northern Madagascar and the Comoros into the wider Swahili-Shirazi network [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar]. Aggregate gridded population more than quadrupled to `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["1100"]])` at 1100AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1400"]])` at 1400AD. Coastal stone towns multiplied: Dembéni (2,68k by 1050AD) on Mayotte, Sima (2,64k peak) and Domoni on Anjouan, Moroni (3,12k by 1300AD) and Iconi on Grande Comore, Mahilaka (6,25k by 1300AD) and Kingany (3,18k) on north-western Madagascar, and Vohemar (3,82k) on the north-east coast exported chloritoschist vessels, rock crystal, mangrove timber and enslaved captives in exchange for Persian Gulf and Chinese ceramics [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. Meanwhile, pastoralists in semi-arid Androy erected walled settlements at Andranosoa (2,94k by 1280AD) and Talaky (1,85k) [@ICM2020MadagascarAtlas].


## Atlantic Sugar Colonies, Mascarene Plantations and Famine Cycles (1460AD to 1810AD)

Between 1400AD and 1700AD, regional gridded population nearly tripled from `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1400"]])` to `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1700"]])`, propelled both by highland rice expansion in Madagascar and by Portuguese Atlantic settlement [@Raison1977PerceptionRealisation; @Seibert2014CrioulizacaoCabo]. In the Gulf of Guinea, São Tomé city expanded from 1,85k in 1520AD to a sugar-boom peak of 6,85k in 1600AD alongside Santo António on Príncipe (2,35k) and the maroon community of São João dos Angolares (1,42k), before Dutch naval attacks and planter flight to Brazil halved urban numbers to 3,2k by 1670AD and 2,45k by 1750AD [@Fonju2021ToticPortuguese; @Dulley2025SobreHistoria; @Berthet2016SaoTome]. In Cabo Verde, Ribeira Grande (Santiago de Cabo Verde, 3,15k peak) and São Filipe on Fogo (3,24k) served as diocesan, administrative and Atlantic slave-provisioning stations, lifting gridded Cabo Verde population to `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["cabo_verde_atlantic"]]$population[["1750"]])` by 1750AD [@Rodrigues2011RecensaoBelinquete; @Pereira2024RecensaoSantos; @Furtado2016CaboVerde].

During the second half of the eighteenth century, severe drought and famine struck the Atlantic and northern Indian Ocean islands. Between 1750AD and 1780AD, Cabo Verde's gridded series contracted by 36%, falling from `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["cabo_verde_atlantic"]]$population[["1750"]])` to `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["cabo_verde_atlantic"]]$population[["1780"]])` during the great famine of the 1770s, while Comoros and São Tomé also dipped slightly, holding total regional population flat between `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["1750"]])` in 1750AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["1780"]])` in 1780AD [@Keese2024BetweenLand; @Ringsmut2026LabantaBraco]. Over the same decades, the Mascarenes surged as French East India Company and royal governors transformed Port-Louis (548 in 1735AD to 14,85k in 1788AD and 24,2k by 1806AD), Saint-Denis (2,42k to 14,6k) and Saint-Paul (2,94k to 13,85k) into bustling commercial ports provisioned by enslaved labour from Madagascar and East Africa [@Oliver1950TheVoyage; @Allen1999SlavesFreedmen; @Larson2000HistoryMemory].

## Merina Unification, Post-Emancipation Sugar Boom and Colonial Entrepots (1810AD to 1895AD)

In the nineteenth century, attested active settlements in the ledger climbed sharply to a peak of 91 around 1860AD (Figure \ref{fig:trends}B), while total gridded population rose from `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1810"]])` in 1810AD to `r viscount_fmt_pop(summary_cache$headline_series[["1830"]])` in 1830AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1890"]])` by 1890AD. In Madagascar, Merina expansion from Alasora and Ambohimanga unified Imerina and subdued Betsileo (founding Fianarantsoa, reaching 9,4k by 1895AD) and the eastern port of Toamasina (10,2k by 1895AD) [@Escamps1858HistoireGeographie; @Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar]. Imerina remained the largest and densest Malagasy sub-region at `r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["merina_central_highlands"]]$population[["1890"]])` (`r viscount_fmt_number(sub_by_id[["merina_central_highlands"]]$end_density_km2, 2L)` persons/km²), followed by Betsileo (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["betsileo_southern_highlands"]]$population[["1890"]])`), Betsimisaraka (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["betsimisaraka_east_madagascar"]]$population[["1890"]])`), Antandroy-Mahafaly (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["antandroy_mahafaly_south_mdg"]]$population[["1890"]])`) and Sakalava (`r viscount_fmt_pop(sub_by_id[["sakalava_menabe_boina"]]$population[["1890"]])`). Mid-century warfare, *fanompoana* conscription and the Franco-Malagasy conflicts produced a modest dip between 1830AD and 1860AD before late-century urban growth resumed at Antananarivo (50k in 1895AD), Mahajanga (14,2k) and Antsiranana (3,45k) [@Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar; @Grandidier1885HistoirePhysique].

```{r tab5-top-centres, results='asis'}
top_12 <- summary_cache$top_settlements[seq_len(min(12L, length(summary_cache$top_settlements)))]
df_t5 <- data.frame(
  Settlement = vapply(top_12, function (s) as.character(s$name), character(1)),
  Territory = vapply(top_12, function (s) as.character(s$country), character(1)),
  Span = vapply(top_12, function (s) {
    if (s$min_year == s$max_year) fmt_era_yr(s$min_year) else paste0(fmt_era_yr(s$min_year), "-", fmt_era_yr(s$max_year))
  }, character(1)),
  `Peak Pop.` = vapply(top_12, function (s) viscount_fmt_pop(s$peak_pop), character(1)),
  `Peak Date` = vapply(top_12, function (s) fmt_era_yr(s$peak_year), character(1)),
  Obs = vapply(top_12, function (s) viscount_fmt_number(s$observation_count, 0L), character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_t5) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_t5,
  "Twelve largest individually assessed settlements across the Western Indian Ocean and Atlantic Islands (500BC to 1895AD).",
  arg3_options = list(label = "tab:top-centres")
)
```

Across the Mascarenes, post-emancipation Indian indentured immigration drove Port-Louis to 74,5k by 1861AD (before malaria outbreaks and railway suburbanisation shifted residents upland to Curepipe 11,3k, Beau-Bassin/Rose-Hill 9,85k, Vacoas/Phoenix 4,85k and Quatre-Bornes 4,12k) and carried Réunion's communes to peaks in 1861AD: Saint-Denis (36,1k), Saint-Pierre (27,8k), Saint-Paul (24,9k), Saint-Benoît (16,2k), Saint-Louis (14,7k) and Saint-André (13,8k) (Table \ref{tab:top-centres}) [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen]. In the smaller archipelagos, Mindelo (6,24k by 1890AD) overtook Praia (4,65k) in Cabo Verde as a British-supplied Atlantic coaling station while labour out-migration reshaped island demographics [@Jung2015MigrationRemittances; @Xin2026EncounteringAutoethnography]; Victoria (6,24k by 1891AD) anchored British Seychelles; Jamestown (2,45k) and Longwood (640) anchored Saint Helena alongside Georgetown on Ascension (310) and Edinburgh of the Seven Seas on Tristan da Cunha (109); and São Tomé recovered to 4,68k by 1878AD as cocoa *roças* revived plantation coercion [@Bussotti2019MarcasDesterro; @Rodrigues2019MultiplasVidas].

# Limitations

Three structural limitations qualify these numbers. First, five-arcminute spatial grids severely attenuate small oceanic islands whose habitable terrain covers only a fraction of an 85 km² grid cell. Consequently, while the gridded Mascarene, Cabo Verde and Gulf of Guinea curves accurately capture relative temporal shocks such as the 1770s famine and nineteenth-century sugar growth, their absolute gridded totals sit well below the full colonial census counts in Table \ref{tab:island-censuses}, and Seychelles and Chagos register zero on the coarse grid despite hosting 10,1k combined urban inhabitants across seven assessed settlements by 1891AD.

Second, pre-colonial Malagasy and Comorian demographic estimates remain far sparser than Mascarene or Portuguese parish records. Outside royal Merina musters and missionary surveys around Antananarivo [@Escamps1858HistoireGeographie; @Grandidier1885HistoirePhysique; @Larson2000HistoryMemory], early coastal centres such as Langany, Boeny, Kingany, Talaky and Dembéni rest on two or three radiocarbon or eyewitness benchmarks [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @ICM2020MadagascarAtlas], and 18 of the 96 gazetteer entries carry single-date late-nineteenth-century colonial observations.

Third, colonial census categories shift across empires and decades. French *compagnie* censuses distinguish free settlers from enslaved labourers differently from post-1848 communal *populations légales*, British Mauritian censuses aggregate Indian-born and Creole populations into shifting district borders [@Allen1999SlavesFreedmen], and Portuguese *fogo* (household) multipliers in Cabo Verde and São Tomé require cautious adjustment during drought emigration and cocoa-estate labour deportations [@Keese2024BetweenLand; @Bussotti2019MarcasDesterro; @Rodrigues2019MultiplasVidas].

# Conclusion

Across nearly two and a half millennia from 500BC to 1895AD, the islands of the western Indian Ocean and the African Atlantic followed two contrasting demographic paths. On Madagascar and the Comoros, early Austronesian and Bantu colonisation gradually filled highland rice basins, western cattle plains and Swahili-linked coral ports, lifting gridded regional population from `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["800"]])` at 800AD to `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1400"]])` by 1400AD and `r viscount_fmt_pop(headline_vals[["1890"]])` across the full study area by 1890AD. On previously uninhabited Atlantic and Mascarene islands, European maritime empire compressed centuries of demographic growth into abrupt plantation booms (São Tomé's sixteenth-century sugar cycle, Cabo Verde's famine-punctuated entrepot economy and the Mascarenes' slave and Indian-indentured sugar expansion) recorded in dense municipal and district censuses. By pairing 492 individually assessed settlements with archival island enumerations and gridded regional series, NICETHI provides a consistent historical foundation for the twentieth-century island chapters that follow.

# Appendix

## Sub-Regional Density and Share Series

Table \ref{tab:density-appendix} reports gridded mean population density in persons per km² across all ten sub-regions from 1AD to 1890AD, highlighting the higher per-kilometre densities of the Mascarenes (`r viscount_fmt_number(sub_by_id[["mascarenes_mauritius_reunion"]]$end_density_km2, 2L)` persons/km²) and Comoros (`r viscount_fmt_number(sub_by_id[["comoros_sultanates_mayotte"]]$end_density_km2, 2L)` persons/km²) relative to arid southern and western Madagascar. Table \ref{tab:shares-appendix} presents each sub-region's percentage share of the gridded regional total, illustrating how Imerina and Betsileo maintained over half of total gridded population across the early modern era while the Mascarenes rose from 0,1% in 1700AD to 2,8% of the coarse grid by 1890AD.

```{r tab6-density-appendix, results='asis'}
dens_rows <- lapply(subregion_order, function (id) {
  sr <- sub_by_id[[id]]
  ar <- as.numeric(sr$area_km2)
  ps <- sr$population
  data.frame(
    Subregion = sr$name,
    `1AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["0"]]) / ar, 2L),
    `800AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["800"]]) / ar, 2L),
    `1400AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["1400"]]) / ar, 2L),
    `1700AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["1700"]]) / ar, 2L),
    `1810AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["1810"]]) / ar, 2L),
    `1890AD` = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(ps[["1890"]]) / ar, 2L),
    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
tot_dens_row <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Mean Study Area",
  `1AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["0"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  `800AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["800"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  `1400AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["1400"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  `1700AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["1700"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  `1810AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["1810"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  `1890AD` = viscount_fmt_number(headline_vals[["1890"]] / total_area_km2, 2L),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_t6 <- rbind(do.call(rbind, dens_rows), tot_dens_row)
rownames(df_t6) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_t6,
  "Mean gridded population density (persons per km²) across the ten sub-regions from 1AD to 1890AD.",
  arg3_options = list(label = "tab:density-appendix")
)
```

# Footnotes

Chronological benchmarks follow astronomical integer conventions in the underlying spatial rasters, where year 0 corresponds to 1AD in historical prose tables. Colonial census aggregates in Table \ref{tab:island-censuses} and Table \ref{tab:mauritius-districts} reflect full island enumerations compiled alongside the 5-arcminute spatial grid, explaining why archival counts for Mauritius, Réunion, Cabo Verde, São Tomé e Príncipe and Seychelles exceed coarse grid-cell totals.
